_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e06 (with v1.0.1's corrected break-even), writer brief a10e06-v1.0.0.md, LATENT catalog v1.0.78 and latent-syllabus-v1.0.3.md. a10e05's next field (only that field was read) was honoured: a tunnel-boring crew under a city, and speculative decoding in plain words, a small helper model guessing the next few words and the big model checking them all at once. Keeps apart from a8e04 (the helper never answers alone; the big model checks every guess and every word is the big model's), from s6e08 (a tunnel under a city: no mine, canary or gas), from the retired fortune-teller setting (no apprentice, no fortunes) and from a10e01's furnace. Shared given data: Llama 3.1 70B, 70.6 billion weights, 80 layers, 141 billion bytes in 16 bits (about 132 GB on the meter), on one machine with two H100 cards (3.35 TB/s each), half the bytes on each: 70.5 / 3,350 = at least 21 ms a token. Thorncliffe's own measurements, never a source's: the big model alone 25 ms a token, 40 a second; the helper, Llama 3.2 1B, 5 ms a guess; a check is one 25 ms read; 80% of guesses kept on the all-English test of Monday 14 September 2026, 30% on Polish questions on Monday 21 September, 40% on English fault-code questions in November; the crew's judgement that the Polish answers are usable. The expected tokens a round, (1 - a^6) / (1 - a), was found in the body of Leviathan, Kalman and Matias (Section 3.1, Equation 1, read on ar5iv) and is credited to them. Story arithmetic (all in sims/a10e06-v1.0.0.js): a round 5 x 5 + 25 = 50 ms; 80%: 3.69 tokens a round, 73.8 a second, 1.84x, a 400-token answer 5.4 s; 30%: 1.43, 28.6 a second, 14.0 s; 50%: 1.97, 39.4; 51%: 2.00, 40.1; break-even 51% kept (0.5087, just over half); 10 guesses: 75 ms rounds, 19.0 a second at 30% (21.0 s), 60.9 at 80%; a 2.5 ms helper: 37.5 ms rounds, 38.1 a second at 30% (10.5 s), break-even 33%; helper off 40 a second, 10.0 s; cold case 40%: 1.66 tokens a round, 33.2 a second. One deliberate change from the brief's draft: tokens a second are shown to one decimal everywhere, so the brief's '19 a second' and '38' read 19.0 and 38.1. Timeline: test Monday 14 September; switched on Tuesday 15 September with the label 'speed-up: on, 1.84x' typed onto the dashboard; every crew asked in English until the Polish subcontractor's crew's first night shift, Monday 21 September from 22:00; Wieslaw radioed at 23:40; the dashboard read at 23:45; the evidence drawn at 00:30 on Tuesday 22 September; the post at about 06:30; the crew back at 22:00 on Tuesday. Cold case: 2 months later, 22 September to Friday 20 November 2026 (the per-language switch from Tuesday 22 September; the fault log linked on Monday 2 November; the slow fault answers on Thursday 19 November). Standards note conditional, not legal advice. Sources read 16 October 2026.
title: The Guess Ahead
setting: a tunnel-boring crew under a city

post.author: u/night_engineer_tsubasa
post.title: I'm the night engineer on a tunnel-boring machine. The dashboard says our assistant's speed-up is on, 1.84 times. Last night it wrote slower than with no speed-up at all.

blocks.text: I'm Tsubasa, night shift engineer on Aroha, the tunnel-boring machine Thorncliffe is driving under Ravensholt: a turning steel cutter as wide as the tunnel, with a moving workshop behind it.
Behind the cutter, the ring-build crew bolts curved concrete pieces into a ring, the tunnel's lining. Then they pump grout, runny concrete, into the gap outside it.
Crews ask our assistant about ring-building steps, grout volumes and fault codes, the machine's numbered alarms.
It's a language model, Llama 3.1 70B, writing each answer in tokens, small pieces of text, one after another.
Its weights, its 70.6 billion learned numbers, take 141 billion bytes of memory.
They sit on two rented graphics cards, NVIDIA H100s, half on each.
To write one token, each card reads its half along its memory road at 3,350 billion bytes a second: at least 21 ms, thousandths of a second. Our own timing: 25 ms a token, 40 tokens a second.

On Monday 14 September Padraig, our IT engineer, tested a helper: a much smaller model, Llama 3.2 1B, that guesses the next token in 5 ms. Like a friend who finishes your sentences, it guesses; the big model decides.

They work in rounds. First the helper guesses 5 tokens, one after another: 25 ms. Then the big model checks all 5 in one read of its weights, 25 ms, the same as writing one token. It keeps the guesses up to the first wrong one and adds one of its own. Every word is still the big model's.

Padraig's test, all English, kept 80% of guesses. A round takes 5 × 5 + 25 = 50 ms. It always gives the big model's own token; the first guess is kept 80% of the time, each later one only if all before it were. By hand: 1 + 0.8 + 0.64 + 0.51 + 0.41 + 0.33 = 3.69 tokens a round. 3.69 ÷ 0.05 s = 73.8 tokens a second, 1.84 times faster.
On Tuesday 15 September he switched it on and typed "speed-up: on, 1.84×" onto the dashboard, the assistant's screen of timings. Every crew since asked in English.

Last night, Monday 21 September, a Polish subcontractor's crew began its first night shift, on ring-build, asking in Polish. Wieslaw, their foreman, says the answers are usable. At 23:40 he radioed me from the ring: answers crawl, and the ring waits.
Each dashboard line: the time, a reading, and what sits beside it. Accepted guesses means kept guesses.

23:45  speed-up: on, 1.84×              typed in 15 Sep, from the 14 Sep test
23:45  accepted guesses, last hour: 30%  day shift: 80%
23:45  tokens a second, last hour: 28.6  helper off, before 15 Sep: 40
On Wieslaw's tablet the words came one at a time, like someone whispering the wrong next word and being told no.

Padraig says the dashboard says 1.84×, so the foreman is just impatient. The Polish crew is back at 22:00 tonight. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing under Ravensholt is haunted, though a voice that hesitates in a tunnel would unsettle anyone. A small model guessing ahead for a big one that checks every guess is called speculative decoding. The share of guesses kept is its acceptance rate. Two questions. When was the 1.84× last measured, and on whose questions? And what was the acceptance rate in that test, and what was it last night?

replies.author: u/night_engineer_tsubasa
replies.text: Once, on Monday 14 September, on English questions only. Nobody has measured it since; it's text Padraig typed. The test kept 80%. Last night, with only the Polish crew asking, 30%.

comments.author: u/it_on_call_padraig
comments.text: I ran the test and I stand by it: 80% kept, 1.84 times faster, on the dashboard in black and white. The words are the big model's either way, so nothing is wrong with the answers. The foreman is just impatient; a new crew on a new machine always is. If you want more speed, let the helper guess 10 ahead: each 25 ms check then covers twice as many tokens.

replies.author: u/night_engineer_tsubasa
replies.text: Does the 1.84× change when the share kept changes?

replies.author: u/it_on_call_padraig
replies.text: It's the test's figure. The test was clean.

comments.author: u/ring_foreman_wieslaw
comments.text: We are not impatient. The Polish is good enough; my crew reads it fine. But a ring answer takes us 14.0 s, against 5.4 s for the English crews on your dashboard, while the whole crew stands at the ring. If the guesser is what's slow, we'd sooner have the plain big model.

replies.author: u/night_engineer_tsubasa
replies.text: Padraig's dashboard still says the English crews get 73.8 tokens a second by day.

comments.author: u/project_manager_mahina
comments.text: Don't throw the 1.84× away. The guessing is the slow part: 25 of every 50 ms. Get a quicker helper and every round shrinks. Or rent faster cards for the big model. I'd rather buy speed than switch a speed-up off.

reply.prompt: It's 06:30 on Tuesday 22 September, and the Polish crew is back at 22:00. What should Thorncliffe change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Let the helper guess 10 tokens ahead so each check covers more of them.
options.part2: On Tuesday afternoon Padraig set the helper to 10 guesses a round. A round became 10 × 5 + 25 = 75 ms. At 22:00 the Polish crew kept 30% of guesses again, so a round still kept about 1.43 tokens: 19.0 tokens a second, and a 400-token ring answer took 21.0 s. By midnight Wieslaw's crew had put the tablets down and was working from the paper manual, and the rings went in slower. On Wednesday the English day crews kept 80%, 4.57 tokens a round: 60.9 tokens a second, down from 73.8. The dashboard still said 1.84×.
options.senior: Guessing further ahead pays only when late guesses are likely to be kept. Guess 6 counts only if guesses 1 to 5 were all kept: at 30%, almost never. Every extra guess still costs the helper 5 ms in every round, so the round grows by half and keeps the same 1.43 tokens. Even at 80% the extra five add under one token for 25 ms more. Set the number of guesses from the measured share kept: few when it is low.

options.text: Turn the helper off for every crew; the big model alone writes 40 a second.
options.part2: On Tuesday Padraig switched the helper off for everyone. At 22:00 the Polish crew got 40 tokens a second; a 400-token ring answer took 10.0 s, and the rings stopped waiting on the tablets. On Wednesday the English day crews got 40 too, not 73.8: their 400-token answers took 10.0 s instead of 5.4 s. Every word was the same as before, because the words were always the big model's. Padraig took the 1.84× off the dashboard.
options.senior: An honest retreat. With the helper off the big model writes as it always did, 25 ms a token, and nothing can be slower than that. The cost is the English crews' speed-up, 73.8 tokens a second back to 40, to fix a fault that lives only in the Polish traffic. It also leaves the real question unasked: on which traffic does the helper pay, and how would you know next time?

options.text: Count kept guesses per language; use the helper only where it pays.
options.part2: On Tuesday Padraig replaced the typed 1.84× with live figures for each language: kept guesses and tokens a second over the last hour. Each crew's tablet already knew its language, so he set a rule from the sim: the helper runs for a language only while its rounds beat the big model alone, which at 5 guesses means just over 50% kept. At 22:00 the Polish questions went straight to the big model: 40 tokens a second, a 400-token ring answer in 10.0 s, and Wieslaw's crew kept their tablets. On Wednesday the English day crews kept 80% and got 73.8 tokens a second, 5.4 s an answer. In both languages every word was the big model's.
options.senior: Speculative decoding is a bet on the helper. Each round pays for its guessing and one check, and wins back only kept guesses. Measure the share kept on each kind of traffic you serve, work out the break-even (here just over 50% for 5 guesses at 5 ms), and switch the helper by traffic. The words never change, only the speed, so the choice can be made on speed alone. Keep the meter live, because the share kept moves with what people ask.

options.text: Swap in a helper twice as fast, 2.5 ms a guess, so rounds get shorter.
options.part2: Mahina's team found a quicker helper, 2.5 ms a guess, and Padraig swapped it in on Tuesday afternoon. A round became 5 × 2.5 + 25 = 37.5 ms. At 22:00 it kept 30% of the Polish crew's guesses, like the old one: 1.43 tokens a round, 38.1 tokens a second, a 400-token ring answer in 10.5 s, still slower than 10.0 s with no helper, and the rings still waited. Nobody had tested the new helper in English, so by Wednesday morning the 1.84× on the dashboard described a helper that was gone, and nobody knew the English crews' speed.
options.senior: A quicker helper shortens the guessing, not the check: every round still holds one 25 ms read of the big model's weights. At 30% kept a round keeps 1.43 tokens whatever the helper's speed, and 1.43 ÷ 0.0375 s is 38.1, below 40. A faster helper lowers the break-even, here to about 33% kept, but the Polish traffic sits below even that. And a new helper is a new change: its share kept must be measured on every kind of traffic before an old test's figure means anything.

sim.title: Count the rounds on Aroha's assistant
sim.lede: You're Tsubasa at 21:59 on Monday 21 September 2026, a minute before the Polish crew's first night shift. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: Llama 3.1 70B, 70.6 billion weights in 80 layers, 141 billion bytes in 16 bits (about 132 GB on the card's meter, where 1 GB is 1,024 MB), on one machine with two H100 cards, half the bytes on each; each card reads its half at 3.35 TB a second (3,350 billion bytes): at least 21 ms a token. Thorncliffe's own timings: the big model alone writes a token every 25 ms, 40 a second; the helper, Llama 3.2 1B, guesses a token in 5 ms; checking a round's guesses takes one 25 ms read. Kept guesses, Thorncliffe's own counts: 80% on Monday 14 September's English test, 30% on tonight's Polish questions. Tokens a round = 1 + the chance each guess is kept (the kept share, times itself once more for each later guess). A ring-build answer is about 400 tokens. The dashboard's speed-up label was typed in on 15 September.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening view is the English day shift: 50 ms rounds, 3.69 tokens a round, 73.8 a second, 1.84 times the big model alone. Play Monday night and watch kept guesses fall to 30%: 1.43 tokens, 28.6 a second, while the dashboard label stays at 1.84×. Set 50% kept, then 51%, to find the break-even. At 30%, try 10 guesses a round, then a 2.5 ms helper. Switch the helper off. Then play each reply, and last, set 40% kept with the helper on for the cold case.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the tunnel was haunted. The helper's guesses are checked in one 25 ms read, but each round also pays 25 ms of guessing. In English 80% of guesses were kept, 3.69 tokens a round, 73.8 a second; in Polish only 30%, 1.43 tokens a round, 28.6 a second, slower than the 40 the big model writes alone. The 1.84× on the dashboard was an English test, typed in once.

steps.title: Writing one token waits on the memory road.
steps.text: First, each H100 reads its half of the big model's weights, 70.5 billion bytes, along its memory road at 3,350 billion bytes a second: at least 21 ms; Thorncliffe measures 25 ms. Second, the adders work out the next token, using each byte about once, so they sit mostly idle (a10e01). Third, the token is added and the read starts again. Because the read is the cost, the same read can check several positions at once for about the same 25 ms. What can go wrong: assuming a check of 5 guesses costs 5 tokens' time, and never trying the trick at all.

steps.title: A guess-and-check round.
steps.text: First, the helper, a much smaller model, guesses 5 tokens one after another at 5 ms each: 25 ms. Second, the big model reads its weights once and, for each of the 5 positions, works out what it would have written itself: 25 ms. Third, it keeps the guesses that match, up to the first one that doesn't. Fourth, it adds one token of its own, so every round gives at least one. Leviathan and colleagues' method also handles drawn-at-random writing, so the output has the same spread of answers as the big model alone. This is speculative decoding; the helper never answers alone, unlike a distilled student (a8e04). What can go wrong: a helper that guesses wrong still spends its 25 ms every round.

steps.title: How many tokens a round keeps.
steps.text: If each guess is kept with the same chance a, the first guess counts a of the time, the second a × a, and so on, plus the big model's own token: 1 + a + a² + a³ + a⁴ + a⁵, which Leviathan and colleagues write as (1 - a^6) ÷ (1 - a), their Equation 1. At 80%: 3.69 tokens a round; ÷ 0.05 s = 73.8 tokens a second, 1.84 times the 40 alone. At 30%: 1.43 tokens, 28.6 a second, 0.71 times. A ring answer of 400 tokens: 5.4 s in English, 14.0 s in Polish, 10.0 s alone. What can go wrong: one test's share standing in for every kind of question.

steps.title: The break-even, and why the other fixes fall short.
steps.text: A 50 ms round must keep 2 tokens to match 40 a second. At 50% it keeps 1.97, 39.4 a second, still below; at 51%, 2.00 tokens, 40.1 a second. So the helper pays only above just over half kept. Guessing 10 ahead makes rounds 75 ms for the same 1.43 tokens: 19.0 a second, and English drops to 60.9. A 2.5 ms helper makes rounds 37.5 ms: 38.1 a second, still below 40, though its break-even falls to 33% kept. A faster card for the big model shortens the check but not the guessing, and leaves 70% of guesses thrown away. What can go wrong: tuning the round while the share kept is the problem.

diagram.aria: The break-even, drawn for 5 guesses at 5 ms and a 25 ms check, a 50 ms round. Top row, by share of guesses kept: 30%, 1.43 tokens a round, 28.6 a second; 50%, 1.97, 39.4 a second; 51%, 2.00, 40.1 a second; 80%, 3.69, 73.8 a second. Bottom row, at 30% kept: 10 guesses, a 75 ms round, 19.0 a second; a 2.5 ms helper, a 37.5 ms round, 38.1 a second; helper off, 25 ms a token, 40 a second.

Break-even: just over 50% kept beats 40 a second alone
The words are the big model's in every box; only the speed changes

fix.title: The fix: count kept guesses per language and use the helper only where it pays
fix.text: Replace the typed 1.84× with live figures for each kind of traffic, here each language: the share of guesses kept and the tokens a second, over the last hour. Work out the break-even for the round you run (just over 50% kept for 5 guesses at 5 ms and a 25 ms check) and switch the helper on only where the live figure beats the big model alone: on for English (73.8 tokens a second), off for Polish (40). Before any new kind of traffic, a new helper or a new number of guesses goes live, measure its share kept on that traffic, in the sim or on recorded questions. The words don't change either way, so the choice is about speed alone.

limits: It pays only while the card has room to spare. vLLM's guide says it helps under medium-to-low QPS (queries per second), memory-bound workloads: when many answers already share each step (a10e04), the adders are busier and checking guesses stops being nearly free. Re-measure at the busiest hour.

The tokens-a-round sum assumes every guess has the same chance of being kept, a simplifying assumption the paper names; real rounds vary, so trust the live tokens a second. The 25 ms, 5 ms, 80% and 30% are Thorncliffe's own measurements, not a source's.

A language is only one kind of traffic: questions within it can differ (the cold case). And the crew judged the Polish answers usable; Polish is not on the Llama 3.1 or 3.2 cards' lists of supported languages, so how good the Polish is needs its own check.

explain.seniorTake: A big model writing one token at a time spends most of each step waiting on its memory road, so one read can check several guessed tokens for about the cost of writing one. Speculative decoding spends that spare room: a small helper guesses a few tokens, the big model checks them all in one read, keeps them up to the first wrong one and adds its own, and the words are exactly what the big model would have chosen. It is a bet, not a free speed-up. Each round pays for the guessing and the check, and wins back only kept guesses, so it pays where the helper guesses well, here English at 80%, and loses where it doesn't, Polish at 30%, slower than no helper at all. More guesses or a quicker helper tune the bet without changing the odds. Measure the share kept on each kind of traffic you serve, keep the helper only where it beats the big model alone, re-measure when traffic, helper or load changes, and never let a test's figure stand on a dashboard as if it were live.

realWorld.title: Leviathan and colleagues: two to three times, the same outputs
realWorld.text: Leviathan, Kalman and Matias's paper (ICML 2023) reports, on T5-XXL: "show a 2X-3X acceleration compared to the standard T5X implementation, with identical outputs." Their measurements, on their models and cards, not Thorncliffe's.

realWorld.title: The same paper: tokens a round
realWorld.text: In Section 3.1 the paper says "the number of tokens produced by a single run of Algorithm 1 is a capped geometric variable," and "the expected number of tokens generated by Algorithm 1 satisfies Equation 1." Equation 1 is the sum the story does by hand, (1 - a^(γ+1)) ÷ (1 - a), with γ guesses; it rests on what the paper calls a "simplifying assumption" that each guess has the same chance. Its introduction promises "guaranteeing that the outputs from our system have the same distribution as those from the target model alone".

realWorld.title: Chen and colleagues: a 70B model
realWorld.text: Chen and colleagues at DeepMind benchmarked the same idea "with Chinchilla, a 70 billion parameter language model", "achieving a 2-2.5x decoding speedup in a distributed setup". A model the size of Thorncliffe's, on their own traffic.

realWorld.title: vLLM: when it helps
realWorld.text: vLLM's Speculative Decoding page says it is used "to reduce inter-token latency under medium-to-low QPS (queries per second), memory-bound workloads", and warns: "Real gains depend on your model family, traffic pattern, hardware, and sampling settings." Thorncliffe's night was a traffic pattern.

realWorld.title: vLLM: the words stay the same
realWorld.text: The same page says "Speculative decoding sampling is theoretically lossless up to the precision limits of hardware numerics." The helper changes how fast the big model's words arrive, not which words.

realWorld.title: Llama's listed languages
realWorld.text: The Llama 3.2 model card says "English, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Hindi, Spanish, and Thai are officially supported." The Llama 3.1 card lists the same eight. Polish is not among them; the story says only that the crew found the answers usable.

realWorld.title: H100: the memory road
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's H100 page gives the H100 SXM a GPU memory bandwidth of 3.35TB/s. Each card reading its 70.5 billion bytes takes at least 21 ms, which is why a check of 5 guesses costs about one token's time.

asked: How does speculative decoding work, and when does it slow things down?
How would you decide whether to turn it on in production?
interview.answer: Writing with a large model is limited by memory bandwidth: every token reads all the weights once, and the compute sits mostly idle, so checking several tokens in one pass costs about the same as writing one. Speculative decoding uses that. A small draft model guesses k tokens, the target model checks them all in one pass, keeps the guesses up to the first mismatch and adds one token of its own; with Leviathan and colleagues' acceptance rule the output distribution is the target model's, so quality doesn't change. Expected tokens per round with acceptance rate a are (1 - a^(k+1)) ÷ (1 - a), and each round costs k draft steps plus one check. On a 70B model at 25 ms a token with a 1B draft at 5 ms and k = 5, 80% acceptance gives 3.69 tokens per 50 ms round, 73.8 tokens a second against 40, and 30% gives 1.43, 28.6 a second, slower than no draft; break-even is just over 50%. It slows things down when acceptance is low (a different language, code, numbers), when k is too large for the acceptance, and when the GPU is already busy with large batches, since the check is no longer nearly free; vLLM says it helps under medium-to-low QPS, memory-bound workloads. To decide for production I'd replay recorded traffic split by kind (language, task), measure acceptance and tokens a second for each at our busiest hour, turn it on only for the kinds that beat the target alone, and keep acceptance and tokens a second on a live dashboard per kind, with an alert when a kind drops below break-even.

terms.def: A machine that digs a tunnel: a turning steel cutter as wide as the tunnel, with a moving workshop behind it that lines the tunnel as it goes. Thorncliffe's is called Aroha.
One band of the tunnel's lining: curved concrete pieces bolted together behind the cutter. The ring-build crew builds one after each push forward.
Runny concrete pumped into the gap between a new ring and the ground around it, so the ring sits firm.
The crew that bolts each ring together and grouts it. On Monday 21 September a Polish subcontractor's crew worked its first night shift on it.
A numbered alarm the machine shows when something goes wrong. Crews ask the assistant what a code means and what to do.
The person who leads a crew on site. Wieslaw leads the Polish ring-build crew.
A firm hired by the main contractor to do part of the work. Thorncliffe hired a Polish subcontractor's crew for night ring-build.
A program that writes text one small piece at a time, having learned from huge amounts of text (a1e01).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes (a1e03). A ring-build answer here is about 400.
The learned numbers a model is made of (a1e02). Llama 3.1 70B has 70.6 billion: 141 billion bytes in 16 bits.
Meta's open-weights language model with 70.6 billion weights and 80 layers: 141 billion bytes in 16 bits, about 132 GB on the card's meter. Thorncliffe's assistant.
Meta's small open-weights language model, about 1.23 billion weights. Thorncliffe uses it as the helper: 5 ms a guess on its own timing.
A board with a GPU, a graphics processing unit, and its own memory: thousands of small adders fed by one fast memory road (a10e01).
A graphics card whose SXM version (the board form built into servers) moves 3.35 TB a second from its memory. Thorncliffe's machine has two, half the weights on each.
This season's word for the link that carries the weights from a card's memory to its adders (a10e01). Its speed sets the shortest time to write one token.
This season's word for the card's many small units that do sums, all at once (a10e01). Writing one token leaves them mostly idle.
A millisecond, a thousandth of a second. The big model writes a token every 25 ms; the helper guesses one in 5 ms.
A much smaller model that guesses the big model's next tokens, like a friend who finishes your sentences. It never answers alone; the big model checks every guess. Engineers call it a draft model.
The engineers' name for the helper: the small model whose guesses the big model checks.
The papers' name for the big model whose words you want, here Llama 3.1 70B. The draft model guesses for it; it checks.
A token the helper writes ahead, before the big model has decided. It counts only if the big model's check agrees.
One turn of guess and check: the helper guesses 5 tokens, the big model checks all 5 in one read, keeps them up to the first wrong one and adds one of its own. 50 ms here.
The big model's one read of its weights in which it works out, for each guessed position, what it would have written itself. 25 ms, the same as writing one token.
Guesses the check agrees with, up to the first wrong one. The dashboard calls them accepted guesses. 80% in Monday's English test, 30% in Polish.
The share of guesses kept, written a in the sums. It decides whether the helper pays.
Writing faster by letting a small model guess a few tokens ahead and the big model check them all in one pass. The words are the big model's; only the speed changes.
On average, 1 + a + a² + ... + a⁵ for 5 guesses kept with share a: (1 - a^6) ÷ (1 - a), Leviathan and colleagues' Equation 1. 3.69 at 80%, 1.43 at 30%.
The share kept at which the helper's rounds match the big model alone: just over 50% (51%) for 5 guesses at 5 ms and a 25 ms check. Below it the helper slows answers.
How fast an answer is written: tokens a round ÷ the round's time. 40 for the big model alone, 73.8 in English with the helper, 28.6 in Polish.
The assistant's screen of timings. Its speed-up line was text typed in from the 14 September test; its kept guesses and tokens a second are live.
Giving the same output as the big model alone, so nothing is lost in quality. vLLM's page says speculative decoding is lossless up to the limits of the card's arithmetic.
Queries per second: how many requests reach the model each second. vLLM says speculative decoding helps under medium-to-low QPS.
T5-XXL is a large language model from Google; T5X is the software Leviathan and colleagues compared against when they measured their speed-up.
DeepMind's language model with 70 billion weights, on which Chen and colleagues measured speculative sampling.
Chen and colleagues' name for the same idea: a draft model proposes tokens and the big model checks them, keeping its own spread of answers.
The International Conference on Machine Learning, one of the main yearly research conferences in the field.

atWork: Look for a speed-up switched on after one test: a draft model, a cache or a shortcut measured on one language or one kind of question, then left on for all traffic. It is a common pattern: the test's figure goes onto a dashboard and stays there while the traffic changes underneath it. Ask four things. Was the speed-up measured on every kind of traffic it now serves, each language and each task? Does the dashboard show the live share of guesses kept and tokens a second, or a figure typed in once? What is the break-even for your round, and which traffic sits below it? And is the card busy enough at peak that checking guesses is no longer nearly free? A later build project will ask you to measure this. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.32 (change management, as summarised by a third-party guide) would look for the change tested on each kind of traffic it serves before release, with the results recorded. An auditor checking SOC 2's CC8.1 (changes to systems), or ISO/IEC 42001:2023's expectations for testing an AI system's change before release, would likely ask the same. How these apply depends on your scope and auditor. This is not legal advice.

recall.prompt: Your team serves a 70-billion-weight model on two GPUs. After a benchmark on English support chats showed answers 1.8 times faster, it turned on a small draft model that guesses 5 tokens ahead. A month later, customers who write in Japanese say answers come slower than before the change. The draft model's acceptance on Japanese chats is 25%. What is happening, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Few guesses are kept, so each round pays for the guessing and the check and gets little back: fewer tokens a second than the big model alone
The benchmark measured only English; measure acceptance and speed for each language or kind of traffic
Use the draft model only where it beats the big model alone; turn it off for that traffic (the words don't change)

recall.model: At 25% acceptance few guesses are kept: a round keeps little more than the big model's own token but still pays for 5 guesses and a check, so the guessing time is wasted and answers come slower than with the big model alone, below the break-even of about half the guesses kept. The benchmark measured only English, where the draft model guesses well. Measure acceptance and tokens a second per language, and per kind of traffic within a language, at a busy hour. Then use the draft model only where it beats the model alone: keep it for English, turn it off for Japanese. The words don't change either way, only the speed.

recall.prompt: A round: the helper guesses 5 tokens at 5 ms each, then the big model checks them in one 25 ms read, keeps them up to the first wrong one and adds one of its own. If 80% of guesses are kept, about how many tokens a second does it write?
recall.why: A round keeps 1 + 0.8 + 0.64 + 0.51 + 0.41 + 0.33 = 3.69 tokens on average and takes 5 × 5 + 25 = 50 ms: 3.69 ÷ 0.05 s = 73.8. 100 counts 4 of 5 guesses kept plus one, forgetting that a wrong guess ends the round; 147.6 forgets the helper's 25 ms of guessing; 40 is the big model alone.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: how does speculative decoding work, and when does it slow things down?

keyIdeas.idea: A small draft model guesses several tokens; the big model checks them all in one pass, keeps them up to the first wrong one and adds its own
Checking costs about the same as writing one token because writing waits on memory, and the output is the big model's own
It pays only when most guesses are kept and the GPU isn't busy; low acceptance, too many guesses or high load make it slower

recall.model: Writing with a big model is memory-bound: every token reads all the weights, so checking several tokens in one pass costs about the same as writing one. A small draft model guesses a few tokens, the big model checks them all in one pass, keeps them up to the first wrong one and adds one of its own; the output has the same distribution as the big model alone, so quality doesn't change. Each round pays for the guessing and the check and wins back the kept guesses, so it pays only when most guesses are kept: on a 70B model at 25 ms a token with 5 guesses at 5 ms, the break-even is just over half. It slows things down when acceptance is low, for example in a language or task the draft model guesses badly, when it guesses too many tokens ahead, or when the GPU is already busy with large batches and the check is no longer nearly free.

recall.prompt: With 5 guesses at 5 ms and a 25 ms check, roughly what share of guesses must be kept before the helper beats the big model's 40 tokens a second alone?
options: Any share: the check is free
recall.why: A 50 ms round must keep 2 tokens to match 40 a second. At 50% it keeps 1.97, 39.4 a second, still below; at 51%, 2.00 tokens, 40.1 a second. 80% was the English test; the check isn't free, it costs one 25 ms read.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. Since Tuesday 22 September the helper has run per language: on for English, off for Polish, with each language's kept guesses live on the dashboard. On Monday 2 November Thorncliffe linked Aroha's fault log to the assistant: when she stops, a crew pastes the fault code and its readings and asks what to do. On Thursday 19 November the English day crew's fault answers crawled, and Mahina asked why the speed-up was slowing them. The dashboard's English line still said helper on, above the break-even. Padraig split the last week by question: questions about fault codes kept 40% of guesses, 33.2 tokens a second. Ring and grout questions still kept about 80%.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are English fault answers slower than with no helper, when the dashboard says the helper pays for English? What would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Questions about fault codes keep only 40% of guesses, below the break-even of just over half: 1.66 tokens a round, 33.2 a second, below 40
Language was only a stand-in for how guessable the text is; an average across a language hides a losing kind, so measure per kind of question
Switch the helper per kind of question: off for fault questions (40 a second), on for ring and grout questions (73.8)

coldCase.model: Language was only a stand-in for how guessable the text is. Fault answers are full of codes and numbers, which are hard to guess for a small helper: 40% kept gives 1 + 0.4 + 0.16 + ... = 1.66 tokens a round, ÷ 0.05 s = 33.2 tokens a second, below the break-even of just over half kept and below the 40 the big model writes alone. The English line still clears break-even because ring and grout questions keep about 80%, so the average hides the losing kind. Measure kept guesses per kind of question, not just per language, and switch per kind: off for fault answers, 40 tokens a second, on for ring and grout questions, 73.8. Keep each kind's live figure on the dashboard, and re-measure whenever a new kind of question arrives.
